What is DeepLense?

Open research on dark matter and strong lensing.

Strong lenses provide a way to study matter that does not emit light. We build models that identify lenses, characterize their morphology, and test how much physical information can be recovered from images.

The work includes simulation, survey-data processing, representation learning, super-resolution, parameter inference, and experimental tools for scientific agents.

Research workflow

From simulated lenses to physical inference.

The group works across the stages needed to connect controlled simulations with astronomical observations.

01

Simulate

Generate controlled lensing systems across candidate dark-matter models.

02

Detect

Identify rare lens candidates in large, noisy astronomical surveys.

03

Model

Train representations using known symmetries, geometry, and lensing physics.

04

Evaluate

Measure what the models recover and how reliably results transfer to survey data.

2025 · Generative simulationPDF ↗

FlowLensing

A conditional flow-matching model for generating strong-lensing images across physical parameters and dark-matter classes.

200×+reported speedup over intensive traditional simulators
2026 · Representation learningPDF ↗

Lens-LeJEPA

A self-supervised model that uses exact lens symmetries and tests when those invariances remove information needed by downstream tasks.

+11.6accuracy points with 100 labels per class
AAAI SpotlightPDF ↗

DLens

A multi-agent framework for coordinating lens simulation, model search, evaluation, and experiment planning through typed interfaces.

8.4×fewer parameters than the comparison ResNet-34

Results above are reported on bounded experimental setups, primarily using simulated data. We distinguish benchmark performance from real-world scientific inference throughout the publication record.

Different measurements require different representations.

A symmetry that improves classification can remove detail needed for reconstruction. A sharper image may not improve a physical estimate. We evaluate models against the scientific task they are intended to support.
